name: CMSIS-NN
baseline: TensorFlow Lite Micro reference kernels (the portable C kernels that TFLM uses when no OPTIMIZED_KERNEL_DIR is set)
workload: TFLM cifar10 example (three convolutional layers; an int8-quantized model is needed for CMSIS-NN to be used) built for the sparkfun_edge target, reference kernels versus TAGS=cmsis-nn, same board, same source tree, timed run in seconds.
claimed_speedup: Third-party issue report: reference kernels 14.05 s and CMSIS-NN 13.13 s with the target Makefile's -fno-builtin (about 1.07x, derived from page data); with -fno-builtin removed, reference 14.01 s versus CMSIS-NN 2.33 s, which the reporter calls 'speeded up by 6x' (about 6.0x, derived from page data). Project README itself gives no numbers, only 'optimized to maximize performance and minimize memory footprint' and 'bit-exact with TensorFlow Lite reference kernels'.
compiler_and_flags: Not fully stated. Build commands on the page: make -f tensorflow/lite/micro/tools/make/Makefile TARGET=sparkfun_edge cifar10_bin, with and without TAGS=cmsis-nn; the only flag discussed is -fno-builtin from apollo3evb_makefile.inc (present vs deleted). GCC version and -O level are not given.
hardware: SparkFun Edge board (Cortex-M4F); the reporter says a Cypress PSoC6 board behaves the same. Clock speed not stated; build host Ubuntu 18.04 under WSL.
stars_or_usage: 449 stars; the CMSIS-NN backend of TensorFlow Lite Micro (tflite-micro tensorflow/lite/micro/kernels/cmsis_nn)
tradeoffs: C library for Cortex-M (DSP extension, Helium/MVE) with int4, int8 and int16 kernels and an experimental float set; bit-exact with TensorFlow Lite reference kernels (TFL and TFLM references may differ, per the README). The README says restrict-keyword and requantize inline-assembly options help some cores (Cortex-M7, Cortex-M4) and not others, and that A-class CPUs are expected to be slower than Arm Compute Library or XNNPACK. IAR is untested.
caveats: Evidence is one March 2020 user issue (opened 2020-03-05, closed 2020-06-11), not a project benchmark: single model, single board, no compiler version or -O level, timing scope (whole run or per inference) not spelled out, and the comparison depends on a TFLM Makefile flag (-fno-builtin) that the TFLM fix PR #37936 later addressed; the CMSIS-NN version then vendored in TFLM is also old. With the flag on, CMSIS-NN was only about 7% faster. The same issue says that from TensorFlow commit 4030aa1 the reference conv and depthwise-conv layers were 'equally fast as the optimized CMSIS-NN kernel or even faster' under that flag, which the reporter traced to -fno-builtin, not to the commit. Other numbers seen only as search-result snippets, pages blocked (EGRESS_BLOCKED) so unverified: the MLSys 2021 TFLM paper (arXiv 2010.08678) reports more than 4x for the Visual Wake Words model on Cortex-M4 and about 25% for the Google Hotword model against reference kernels; an Arm blog reports 3.1x with GCC on a Cortex-M7 (2.26 versus 0.72 inferences/s); the original 2018 CMSIS-NN paper (arXiv 1801.06601) reports 4.6x runtime on CIFAR-10 on a Cortex-M7 at 216 MHz, but against a Caffe-like baseline built on CMSIS-DSP 1D convolution, not TFLM reference kernels. A tflite-micro pull request opened 2026-10-10 (#3823, float32 Conv2D dispatch, page opened) quotes total CONV_2D ticks 235.6M down to 19.1M (about 12.35x) on the Corstone-300 FVP, which it says is not cycle accurate; core, compiler and flags not stated. The CMSIS-NN README and release notes carry no cycle counts or speedups.

name: Rust-for-CPP-Developers: matrix_multiply_indexing_opt (accumulator hoisted into a local sum)
baseline: naive nested-loop matrix multiply with in-place accumulation (out[i][j] += a[i][k]*b[k][j]), same language (the repo's matrix_multiply_original)
workload: 100x100 f32 Vec<Vec<f32>> matrix multiply, Criterion benchmark, naive triple loop versus the same loop with the running sum kept in a local variable and stored once.
claimed_speedup: Book-reported (per the lead): about 2.24 ms down to about 540 microseconds, a 75.9 percent improvement (about 4.1x, derived from the quoted figures).
compiler_and_flags: Criterion 0.5 via cargo bench (release profile, [profile.release] debug = true in Cargo.toml); Rust 1.82.0 or newer per the book, nightly toolchain for the SIMD step (portable_simd); no RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu stated.
hardware: Not stated (author's own machine per the book).
stars_or_usage: 11 stars (Packt companion repository for the book Rust for C++ Developers)
tradeoffs: Safe Rust, same API and result type; pure source-level change in the inner loop; still bounds-checked and still strides down b's columns (no transpose or blocking).
caveats: Baseline is the book's own deliberately naive Rust version, so this is a small idiom fix, not a library win. The repo carries the code for this step (chapter_10/src/lib.rs, chapter_10/src/simd.rs, Criterion bench chapter_10/benches/multiply.rs, Cargo.lock pins criterion 0.5.1 and rand 0.8.5) but no benchmark results, no CPU and no compiler version; the quoted timings come only from the book text as paraphrased in the lead and appear on no page opened here, so they are first-party and unverified. The bench times only the alias matrix_multiply (the unsafe-indexing version on a default build; the SIMD version with --features nightly) and its closure clones both 100x100 input matrices and allocates the Vec<Vec<f32>> result inside the timed region, which dilutes every step; reproducing the earlier steps needs editing the alias in lib.rs. All three steps compare Rust against its own earlier Rust version; no BLAS, ndarray, nalgebra or C++ baseline appears anywhere in the repo (derived: 2*100^3 flops in 208 microseconds is about 9.6 GFLOPS, in 2.24 ms about 0.9 GFLOPS). The repo has only 3 commits, 11 stars, and no tests that check the results.

name: Rust-for-CPP-Developers: matrix_multiply_simd (std::simd f32x4 inner product)
baseline: same-language scalar unsafe-indexing matrix multiply (the repo's matrix_multiply_unsafe_indexing)
workload: 100x100 f32 Vec<Vec<f32>> matrix multiply, Criterion benchmark via cargo +nightly bench, scalar get_unchecked loop versus a 4-lane std::simd f32x4 dot product with a horizontal swizzle-add.
claimed_speedup: Book-reported (per the lead): improved by about 41 percent to roughly 208 microseconds versus the scalar unsafe-indexing version (about 1.7x versus 359 microseconds, derived from the quoted figures); cumulative about 2.24 ms to 208 microseconds (about 10.8x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Criterion 0.5 via cargo bench (release profile, [profile.release] debug = true in Cargo.toml); Rust 1.82.0 or newer per the book, nightly toolchain for the SIMD step (portable_simd); no RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu stated.
hardware: Not stated (author's own machine per the book).
stars_or_usage: 11 stars (Packt companion repository for the book Rust for C++ Developers)
tradeoffs: Needs nightly Rust (portable_simd) behind the nightly cargo feature. The b matrix is not transposed, so each lane group is gathered with four strided loads; matrix sizes must be multiples of four.
caveats: Code check: simd.rs loops p in steps of 4 and skips any tail (if p + 4 <= a_cols), so a shared dimension that is not a multiple of four silently drops terms and returns a wrong product; the speedup holds only for the multiple-of-four case the benchmark uses. Baseline is the book's own scalar Rust, not an optimized library. The repo carries the code for this step (chapter_10/src/lib.rs, chapter_10/src/simd.rs, Criterion bench chapter_10/benches/multiply.rs, Cargo.lock pins criterion 0.5.1 and rand 0.8.5) but no benchmark results, no CPU and no compiler version; the quoted timings come only from the book text as paraphrased in the lead and appear on no page opened here, so they are first-party and unverified. The bench times only the alias matrix_multiply (the unsafe-indexing version on a default build; the SIMD version with --features nightly) and its closure clones both 100x100 input matrices and allocates the Vec<Vec<f32>> result inside the timed region, which dilutes every step; reproducing the earlier steps needs editing the alias in lib.rs. All three steps compare Rust against its own earlier Rust version; no BLAS, ndarray, nalgebra or C++ baseline appears anywhere in the repo (derived: 2*100^3 flops in 208 microseconds is about 9.6 GFLOPS, in 2.24 ms about 0.9 GFLOPS). The repo has only 3 commits, 11 stars, and no tests that check the results.

name: CUTLASS
baseline: cuBLAS (cublasSgemm, run through the CUDA samples' matrixMulCUBLAS)
workload: Single-precision GEMM, m=640, n=320, k=480 (196,608,000 flops), CUTLASS profiler kernel sgemm_tt versus the CUDA sample matrixMulCUBLAS on the same GTX 1080, posted by a user in a 2018 issue.
claimed_speedup: No speedup in the independent data: CUTLASS sgemm_tt 2840.5 GFLOPS (0.069216 ms) versus cuBLAS 3065.46 GFLOPS (0.064 ms), about 92.7% of cuBLAS throughput (derived from page data); the reporter says 'similar results to cublas' and a CUTLASS developer calls sgemm 'comparable to the kernel launched in the CUDA SDK example'. The project's own README claim (CUTLASS 2.x/3.x versions) is 'peak performance comparable to cuBLAS for scalar GEMM', shown only as a chart.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 9.2 toolkit and samples; compiler flags not stated on the page. README charts: CUTLASS 3.0 built with CUDA 12.0 and CUTLASS 3.5.1 with CUDA 12.5u1; flags not stated.
hardware: GeForce GTX 1080 (compute capability 6.1) in the issue. README chart versions name NVIDIA H100, L40, A100 and A40 GPUs.
stars_or_usage: 10.7k stars; the template layer under many deep-learning GPU kernels
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ CUDA template library (CuTe, plus Python DSLs in version 4); kernels are classes with many template arguments, so compile times are long and a kernel must be instantiated per data type, layout, tile shape and architecture; per-architecture tuning (Hopper, Blackwell) is left to the user or the profiler. Offers fusions and epilogues that a closed cuBLAS call cannot.
caveats: Not a faster-than-baseline result: the only measured head-to-head found is slightly slower than cuBLAS, so this entry is kept as a parity claim. The measurement is a single 2018 user post (issue opened and closed on 2018-05-21) on a small problem where launch overhead is large, one run per tool, harness timers differ (profiler versus matrixMulCUBLAS), CUDA 9.2 and an old CUTLASS release, no compiler flags. The issue's CUTLASS dgemm lines used a mismatched shape (m=640, n=480, k=320) and are not comparable. README figure for version 3.0 (opened via the v3.0.0 README, bars read by eye and not printed numbers) shows relative peak performance of roughly 85 to 100 percent per data type and layout on A100, A40, H100 and L40; the README text says 'relative to cuBLAS' but the axis is titled relative peak performance of GEMM, and the current README no longer carries any cuBLAS comparison (it shows percent of theoretical peak on Blackwell and Hopper). The v3.4.0 README figure is CUTLASS 3.1 versus 3.0, not versus cuBLAS. Several NVIDIA libraries, cuBLAS included, build on CUTLASS-style kernels, so parity is expected. A third-party page quoting 235+ TFLOPS for FP16 on H100 was blocked here and not used. The book lead says the book benchmarks its own kernel against cuBLAS, not CUTLASS; no book numbers used.
